chapters.title: Chapter 2: Working Capital and the Cash Conversion Cycle

lessons.title: The Cash Conversion Cycle: Inventory Days, Receivable Days and Payable Days

children.text: Lesson 2.1 measured working capital in rupees. Rupees are hard to compare: ₹3 crore is crushing for one business and trivial for another. Days are better. The cash conversion cycle turns your working capital into a single number of days, and that number answers the only question that matters to a cash manager: how long does my money stay out of my hands before it comes back?

body.text: The cash conversion cycle is the number of days your money is out of the bank and inside the business. Cut the days and cash appears, without a single extra sale.

children.text: The cycle has three parts. Two of them work against you and one works for you.

body.text: Stretching DPO is a real lever, but it has a hard floor. Paying a micro or small supplier beyond the MSMED Act limit is not clever cash management, it carries interest and a tax consequence. Lesson 3.2 covers exactly where that line sits.

children.text: Back to the Morbi tile maker from Lesson 2.1: sales of ₹12 crore, cost of goods sold of ₹8.4 crore, inventory of ₹1.8 crore, receivables of ₹2.4 crore and payables of ₹1.2 crore.

children.text: Count the gap between Day 52 and Day 151. That is 99 days during which Konkan Ceramics has paid for the tiles and not been paid for them. Somebody has to fund those 99 days, every day of the year, on every batch in the system.

body.text: More than a quarter of this company's profit is being handed to a bank as the price of its own slow cycle. Nobody in the business can see that cost, because it arrives as one interest line, far away from the decisions in sales and procurement that caused it.

body.title: Mind the sign
body.textWithBlank: In the cash conversion cycle formula, days payables outstanding is ___ from the total.
body.explanation: Supplier credit is funding you receive, so it shortens the period your own cash is committed. Inventory days and receivable days lengthen it. That single minus sign is why negotiating supplier terms has exactly the same cash effect as collecting faster.

children.text: Days only change behaviour once somebody converts them into money. The conversion is simple.

body.caption: Use sales per day for receivable days, and cost of goods sold per day for inventory and payable days

children.text: For Konkan Ceramics, one day of sales is ₹12 crore divided by 365, about ₹3.3 lakh. One day of cost of goods sold is ₹8.4 crore divided by 365, about ₹2.3 lakh. Now a target-setting conversation becomes concrete.

stats.label: Cash released
stats.context: Without one extra rupee of sales

stats.label: Working capital falls
stats.context: Cash that returns to the bank

body.text: Compare the two routes to ₹91 lakh of cash. At a 10% net margin, generating it as profit needs ₹9.1 crore of additional sales, which means new dealers, new capacity and more risk. Or you collect 13 days faster, hold 13 days less stock and pay 8 days later. The second route is available to almost every business, starting on Monday.

body.title: What is a day worth?
body.prompt: A distributor has annual sales of ₹36.5 crore. Its collections team reduces days sales outstanding by 10 days, with no change in sales, stock or supplier terms. How much cash does that release, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹36.5 crore divided by 365 is exactly ₹10 lakh of sales a day. Ten days of collections released is 10 times ₹10 lakh, which is ₹1 crore of cash, permanently, as long as the new discipline holds. This is why collections targets are usually stated in days, not rupees.

body.title: Sales or cost of goods sold in the denominator?

children.text: You will see both used, and the difference matters when you compare two companies.
are billed at selling price, so they belong over sales. Strictly, over credit sales only, though most published figures use total sales because the split is rarely disclosed.
are recorded at cost, so they belong over cost of goods sold. Purchases is technically better for payables, but COGS is used far more often because purchases are not separately disclosed.

Two practical warnings. First, mixing conventions inflates or deflates the cycle, so check what your finance team used before comparing against last year. Second, all of these use year-end balances, which can be tidied up just before 31 March. A month-end average across the year is far harder to dress up, and far more useful to manage with.
The Same Cycle Across Four Real Businesses
Sector shapes the cycle far more than management skill does. These are consolidated figures from screener.in for the year ended March 2026, alongside our fictional tile maker.

body.caption: Cash conversion cycle, year ended March 2026 (days, as reported on screener.in)

body.title: Where the days sit, year ended March 2026

children.text: Three very different shapes. Titan is almost entirely an inventory business, because gold and finished jewellery must sit in hundreds of stores while customers pay at the counter. Asian Paints runs a balanced cycle and uses strong supplier terms, 79 days, to offset its stock. TCS has no inventory at all, so its cycle is purely a collections story, and at 93 days its cash is tied up as long as the tile maker's.

body.text: Never benchmark a cycle across sectors. A 93-day cycle is normal for IT services billing large enterprises and would be alarming for a restaurant. Compare a business against its own history and its direct competitors, nothing else. Published component figures are also rounded, so they may not add exactly to the reported cycle.

body.title: Read the trend
body.question: A components maker reports a cash conversion cycle of 64 days, up from 51 days last year. Inventory days are flat and payable days are flat. What is the most likely explanation, and what should you check first?
options: Sales have fallen, so check the order book
Debtor days have risen by about 13, so check the receivables ageing report
The company has repaid debt, so check the loan schedule
Depreciation has increased, so check the fixed asset register
body.explanation: The cycle has only three moving parts. If inventory days and payable days are unchanged, the entire 13-day rise sits in debtor days. Debt repayment and depreciation do not enter the cycle at all. The first document to ask for is always the receivables ageing, broken down by customer.

body.title: The dealer who wants 90 days
body.scenario: Konkan Ceramics' largest dealer, worth ₹2 crore of annual sales, asks to move from 60-day to 90-day credit. He is a reliable payer and hints that a competitor has offered him the same. Your sales head wants to agree immediately. The company borrows on cash credit at 11%.
body.prompt: Price the request in cash terms, then decide what you would offer.
body.modelAnswer:
Price it first.
1. ₹2 crore of annual sales is about ₹55,000 a day (₹2 crore divided by 365).
2. Thirty extra days ties up roughly 30 times ₹55,000, about ₹16.4 lakh of additional cash, permanently, for as long as he stays on those terms.
3. At 11%, funding that costs about ₹1.8 lakh a year.
4. Set that against the gross margin on ₹2 crore of sales. If the margin is comfortably above ₹1.8 lakh, and it almost certainly is, the deal is affordable. Affordable is not the same as free.
Then decide what to trade for it.
5. Never give credit terms away for nothing. Ask for something back: a higher volume commitment, a price increase of about 1%, or exclusivity in his territory.
6. Offer alternatives that cost less cash: 75 days rather than 90, or 90 days only in the festive quarter when he genuinely needs stock early.
7. Check whether bill discounting or a channel finance arrangement through the bank can fund the extra 30 days more cheaply than your own cash credit, so he gets 90 days and you get paid in 5.
8. Confirm the headroom exists. If the cash credit limit is already stretched, ₹16.4 lakh matters more than the arithmetic suggests.
9. Whatever is agreed, write it into the dealer agreement with a defined consequence for late payment, and review it after two quarters.

body.title: Calculate your own cycle this week
steps: Pull sales, cost of goods sold, inventory, trade receivables and trade payables from the last audited financials.
Calculate DIO, DSO and DPO using the formulas above, and note which denominator you used for each.
Add DIO and DSO, then subtract DPO to get the cycle in days.
Repeat the calculation for the previous two years and look only at the direction of travel.
Convert one day into rupees: sales divided by 365, and cost of goods sold divided by 365.
Ask each function for a realistic target for the coming year, and multiply the days saved by the rupee value of a day.
Put that single rupee number in front of the management team. Days do not motivate anyone. Cash does.

cards.definition: Days inventory outstanding. Inventory divided by cost of goods sold, times 365. How long stock sits before it sells.
Days sales outstanding. Receivables divided by sales, times 365. How long customers take to pay.
Days payables outstanding. Payables divided by cost of goods sold, times 365. How long you take to pay suppliers.
DIO plus DSO minus DPO. The days your own cash funds the business.
Sales or cost of goods sold divided by 365. Converts days saved into rupees released.
A report splitting what each customer owes by how overdue it is. The first document to ask for when DSO rises.

points: The cash conversion cycle is DIO plus DSO minus DPO: the days between paying for goods and being paid for them.
Konkan Ceramics funds a 99-day gap, and the interest on it swallows about 28% of its annual profit.
Convert days into rupees before setting any target. One day is sales, or cost of goods sold, divided by 365.
Cutting the cycle from 99 to 65 days releases about ₹91 lakh, the same cash that ₹9.1 crore of extra sales would have produced.
All three levers matter equally. Eight days from suppliers is worth as much as eight days from customers.
Cycles are sector-specific. Titan runs 211 days, Asian Paints 84 and TCS 93. Compare a company only with its own history and its direct rivals.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional. Titan, Asian Paints and TCS figures are consolidated ratios from screener.in as published at the time of writing, and may be restated later. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
